boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Eschenau entry (20 October 1805) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1805 group: the pursuit fights of Murat's cavalry under General Klein against Archduke Ferdinand's force from beyond Nuremberg by Heroldsberg to Eschenau and Forth, until nightfall. The march of 19 October by Gunzenhausen, the cavalry's escape to Pegnitz and Eger and the totals of Murat's five-day pursuit are context; the totals are recorded as such and not attributed to this engagement. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side B (Austrian) under Archduke Ferdinand as 3,000 men and prints no strength for side A (French) under Marshal Prince Murat. By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. He does not say which of the Archduke's troops he counted, and the passages read do not say which figures he used (claims krauss-side-b and side-b-french-figures). English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the entry: 'victory of the French under Marshal Prince Murat over the Austrians (3,000 men) under Archduke Ferdinand of Austria'.

claims.value: Side B (Austrian) in Krauss: the march table for 19 October, issued at Öttingen on the 18th, gives the Archduke's troops as 3 battalions, 4 divisions and 28 squadrons. On the 20th the Austrians continued their retreat by Nuremberg toward Eschenau; the remainder of their infantry was worn out by the unbroken march in pouring rain.
claims.rationale: Side B's march table as Krauss summarizes it from the Kriegsarchiv, read from the page image; it counts units for the day before, not men on the 20th, and the passages read give no Austrian return of men for the action. The force reached Eschenau as it stood after the retreat, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): 'the strength of the Archduke's troops was therefore: 3 battalions, 4 divisions, 28 squadrons (Kriegsarchiv ...; march table for 19 October. Öttingen, 18 October 1805)'; 'on the 20th the Austrians continued the retreat by Nuremberg to Eschenau'; 'in these fights the rest of the Austrian infantry, which was completely exhausted by the uninterrupted march in pouring rain, was dispersed and taken prisoner'.

claims.value: Side B (Austrian), side A's figures: the dragoon division's record says the day cost the enemy the rest of his infantry, consisting of 1500 men; the cavalry reserve's report and Alombert and Colin say Archduke Ferdinand got away with 3,000 to 4,000 horsemen.
claims.rationale: Side A's figures, read from the page images; they describe what was taken and what escaped, not a count of side B before the action, and are not added together here. English renderings (ours): the record, 'this brilliant day cost the enemy the rest of his infantry, consisting of 1500 men, 600 horses of different regiments, 33 guns, his caissons and his baggage'; the report, 'all that was not taken prisoner, except 3,000 to 4,000 men of cavalry who follow Archduke Ferdinand, has been scattered in the woods, without arms and without food'; Alombert and Colin, 'Archduke Ferdinand still managed to escape with 3,000 or 4,000 horsemen'.

claims.value: Side A engaged its cavalry: Klein's advance guard of the 1st hussars and the Guard chasseurs caught the Austrian rear beyond Nuremberg, and the dragoon division and the carabiniers came up for the attack at Eschenau. Klein had left the tired infantry behind. The cavalry reserve's report sums up the five days' pursuit as the work of an army corps of 7.000 men; no passage read gives the strength of the troops engaged on the 20th.
claims.rationale: Krauss's account, read from the page image, and the dragoon division's record (OCR); the report's 7.000 is printed with a full stop and covers Murat's whole corps over five days, including the infantry that did not fight here, so it is not the engaged strength. Klein's decision to go on with the cavalry alone sets the tag. English renderings (ours): Krauss, 'hardly had the Austrians passed Nuremberg when their tail was caught up by General Klein's advance guard (1st hussar regiment and Guard chasseurs)'; 'after the arrival of the dragoon division and the carabiniers Klein advanced against the main body of the Austrians standing at Eschenau'; the record, 'but, noticing that the infantry, tired, was slowing the march, he ordered the cavalry to increase its pace and to leave it behind'; the report, 'in five days an army corps of 7.000 men has, in a march of 45 leagues, destroyed a corps of 25,000 men, taken 12,000 or 15,000 prisoners, among them 9 general officers, taken 128 guns, 11 flags, 500 or 600 wagons, the treasury of the Austrian army, which was plundered, and a great quantity of baggage'.

claims.value: On the 20th Murat let the enemy go ahead and set his army moving only at 8 o'clock. General Klein, told that the enemy was only a few hours ahead, wanted to catch it quickly before it could cut the bridge over the Rednitz; finding that the tired infantry slowed the march, he had the cavalry quicken its pace and leave the infantry behind, and informed Murat. At Nuremberg he had the column close up and put the hussars, Guard chasseurs and carabiniers to the trot; his advance guard attacked at once, took 500 men and fell on the artillery train. When the enemy rallied in force near Eschenau, Klein ordered the chasseurs to wait for more troops; the two carabinier regiments, followed by the dragoons, then made three charges, the third and decisive one near Forth.
claims.rationale: Decisions of side A's commanders as Alombert and Colin, the dragoon division's record and Krauss give them (page images, except the record's passages on Klein's intentions and the trot, seen in the OCR). English renderings (ours): Alombert and Colin, 'on 20 October Murat lets the enemy take the lead, and sets his army in motion only at 8 o'clock'; the record, 'General Klein, informed that the enemy was preceding us by only a few hours, wished to reach him promptly and not to give him time to cut the bridge over the Rednitz near the village of Rüttonbach (OCR); but, noticing that the infantry, tired, was slowing the march, he ordered the cavalry to increase its pace and to leave it behind; he informed Prince Murat of this disposition'; 'the divisional general had word sent to the tail to close up, and at once he put the hussars, the Guard chasseurs and the carabiniers to the trot and moved against the enemy'; Krauss, 'Klein had them attack at once, took 500 men prisoner and then threw himself on the artillery train'; the record, 'the enemy having rallied near the village of Eschenau and being in force, General Klein ordered the chasseurs to wait for the arrival of new troops to attack him; the two regiments of carabiniers, followed by the dragoons, were not long in arriving and made three charges with the greatest success; the third, which was decisive, took place near the village of Forth'.

claims.value: Archduke Ferdinand commanded side B, retreating by Nuremberg toward Eschenau. Its rear tried to check the pursuit with guns put into battery on the height of Geschaid, and near Eschenau the main body, rallied and in force, brought six guns into action before it was thrown back. The Archduke escaped on the horse of one of his officers; his cavalry continued the retreat in the night by Gräfenberg to Pegnitz. From Schwabach he wrote to Hohenzollern that the French general's claims were illegal and that Hohenzollern and the troops who had come back with him could not be included in Werneck's capitulation.
claims.rationale: Side B's conduct as Krauss and side A's accounts give it (page images, except the guns on the heights, the Archduke's escape and his letter, seen in the OCR). The passages read do not show the Archduke deciding to stand at Eschenau, so the claim is not tagged commander_created. The letter bears on Werneck's capitulation (B365d). English renderings (ours): Krauss, 'although these brought six guns into fire, they were thrown back and the guns taken'; 'the Austrian cavalry continued the retreat that same night by Gräfenberg to Pegnitz'; Alombert and Colin, 'the most serious fight began near Heroldsberg, where the light cavalry made three (OCR) very brilliant charges and carried the pursuit as far as Eschenau in spite of some guns put into battery by the enemy on the height of Geschaid'; the record, as in claim side-a-command; the report, 'Archduke Ferdinand had only the time to mount the horse of one of his officers to save himself: it was night'; the Archduke, 'you have submitted to me the letter of Lieutenant General Werneck; I shall answer you that according to the laws of war and the rights of nations I find the claims of the French general very illegal. Consequently I declare that you and the troops with which you came back cannot be included in the capitulation. I therefore order you, and them, to continue to serve as before'.

claims.value: Bodart records a victory of side A (French) over side B (Austrian). Side A's accounts say the day gave the last blow to what remained of the corps that had left Ulm, and Krauss that the rest of the Austrian infantry was dispersed and taken, while the Archduke escaped with his cavalry. No source read gives a different result.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome with the agreeing statements of both sides' accounts (page images, except the report's sentence and Alombert and Colin's, seen in the OCR). English renderings (ours): Bodart, 'victory of the French'; the report, 'this day dealt the last blow to the rest of the enemy corps that had come out of Ulm'; Alombert and Colin, '[the two regiments] pursued as far as Forth, where night and weariness ended the fight. The rest of the enemy's materiel and infantry fell into our hands that day'; Krauss, as in claim krauss-side-b; Alombert and Colin, as in claim side-b-french-figures.

claims.rationale: Bodart's printed loss, rounded up by his rule (claim bodart-strength); the dash in the French column marks no figure. A post-outcome observation. English rendering (ours): 'Austrian loss: 1,500 men, 23 guns'.

claims.value: Side B's loss in the other accounts: Krauss says Klein took 1500 prisoners and 33 guns that day, 500 of the prisoners when he first caught the rear; the dragoon division's record gives the rest of the infantry, 1500 men, 600 horses, 33 guns, caissons and baggage, and in the decisive charge all the artillery, General Mecsery, many officers and about 200 horses; the cavalry reserve's report lists as the trophies of the 'combat of Nuremberg' 35 guns, the only ones the enemy had left, more than 100 vehicles or caissons, 5 field forges, 400 horses and as many horsemen, 500 or 600 prisoners including General Mecsery, dangerously wounded, several officers of note and two flags. Alombert and Colin say 1500 infantry were taken in the woods, but that, sent back to Nuremberg, they could not be guarded there and many escaped.
claims.rationale: Separate accounts, read from the page images and not combined; the figures differ and may count different things (the report's '400 horses and as many horsemen' beside 500 or 600 prisoners). Dupont's division journal gives another set of figures, seen only in the OCR and not restated, and says the Prussian troops enlisted many of the prisoners. English renderings (ours): Krauss, 'Klein took 1500 prisoners and 33 guns on this day', and as in claim side-a-command; the record, as in claims side-b-french-figures and side-a-command, '... with the loss of all his artillery, of General Mecsery, of many officers of all ranks and of about 200 horses'; the report, '35 pieces of artillery, the only ones he had left, more than 100 vehicles or caissons, 5 field forges, 400 horses, as many horsemen, 500 or 600 prisoners, among them a general, General Mecsery, who is dangerously wounded, several officers of note and two flags are the trophies of the combat of Nuremberg'; Alombert and Colin, 'the 1st hussars, the Guard chasseurs and the carabiniers then set off again at the gallop; 1500 enemy infantry were taken in the woods; unfortunately, sent back to Nuremberg, they could not be guarded there, and many escaped'; Dupont's journal, 'the Prussian troops, who recruit from foreigners, took good care not to miss so good an opportunity to fill their ranks'.

claims.value: Side A's loss in its own accounts: the cavalry reserve's report gives 11 wounded, among them the colonel of the 1st carabiniers; the dragoon division's record gives about twenty men wounded, among them Colonel Cochois of the 1st carabiniers, with 10 horses killed and 30 wounded. Bodart prints no loss for side A.
claims.rationale: Two side A accounts, read from the page images; they differ (11 or about twenty wounded) and are not reconciled here. open_questions: Deferred: the Archduke's and his generals' reports of the action; the full march table (Kriegsarchiv, 1805, Deutschland FA, X, 166½), which Krauss summarizes; Dupont's division journal for 20 October (t. III, vol. 2, p. 1256), whose figures were seen only in the OCR; Murat's report of 22 October, whose totals Krauss gives (p. 493, OCR). Figures seen only in the OCR and not restated in values: the hour the cavalry reserve's report gives for the start (which differs from Alombert and Colin's 8 o'clock on the page image); the report's figures for the dragoons pushed back beyond Nuremberg and for the league count; Krauss's daily distances (p. 493).

Most consequential gap: side B's strength in the action. Bodart's 3,000 is unexplained; Krauss's march table counts units for 19 October, and side A's figures give 1500 infantry lost and 3,000 to 4,000 cavalry escaping. Krauss's Eger returns (p. 492) concern the cavalry and artillery after the retreat. An Austrian return for 20 October could close it.

Disputes recorded in the claims: side B's loss as 1,500 men and 23 guns (Bodart), 1500 prisoners and 33 guns (Krauss, the dragoon division's record) or 35 guns and 500 or 600 prisoners (the cavalry reserve's report); side A's wounded as 11 (the report) or about twenty (the record).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked); Alombert and Colin, t. III (the French official history, printing the cavalry reserve's report, the dragoon division's record and Dupont's division journal, all interested accounts, and the Archduke's letter to Hohenzollern; its introduction summarizes them); Krauss (an Austrian history drawing on the Kriegsarchiv for side B's march table and returns; his figures for the day's captures agree with the dragoon record and may rest on it).
